sections.heading: 1757–1856: from trading company to paramount power

blocks.text: In a single century the East India Company converted trade posts into an empire through **war, diplomacy and annexation**. The hinge events: **Plassey (23 June 1757)** — Siraj-ud-Daula betrayed by **Mir Jafar**; Bengal's wealth opened; **Buxar (1764)** — the real military decision, defeating Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daula + Shah Alam II together; the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** granted the Company the **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa** — revenue collection = sovereignty's substance. Then the **dual government (1765-72)** — power without responsibility — collapsed into the 1770 Bengal famine (a third of Bengal perished).

rows: Superior artillery-infantry drill + Indian sepoys + naval control
Anglo-Mysore wars (4; **Tipu fell at Srirangapatnam, 1799**), Anglo-Maratha wars (3; ended 1818 — Peshwa abolished), Anglo-Sikh wars (2; **Punjab annexed 1849**)
British troops stationed at the ally's cost; Resident at court; no other Europeans; foreign policy surrendered
**Hyderabad first (1798)** — the Nizam's state became the model client; then Mysore, Awadh, the Marathas
No adopted heir recognised; state 'lapses' to the Company
**Awadh (1856)** — the sepoys' homeland; the deepest 1857 grievance
Carnatic wars' nawab-making; Maratha internal feuds

sections.heading: Why the British won — and what rule meant

items: **Causes of success**: disciplined drilled infantry & standardised artillery; naval supremacy (reinforcement + trade); Bengal's revenues funding wars (Indian resources conquered India); unified command vs fractured Indian polities; the sepoy army (Indians ~5/6 of Company forces); contractual credit networks (Jagat Seths' finance); and no pan-Indian identity yet to resist as one.

**Consolidation architecture (1773-1856)**: Regulating Act 1773 (Governor-General; Supreme Court 1774) → Pitt's India Act 1784 (Board of Control — dual control) → Charter Acts 1813 (trade monopoly ends, ₹1 lakh for education), 1833 (Governor-General **of India**; law commission — Macaulay), 1853 (open competition for civil service) — the legal scaffolding of empire.

**Economic meaning**: 'Plassey plunder' → drain of wealth (**Dadabhai Naoroji's** later theorisation); deindustrialisation of textiles; land settlements re-engineering agrarian society (next note); India as raw-material supplier and captive market — **colonialism's three stages** (mercantile plunder → free-trade exploitation → finance imperialism, per R.P. Dutt's framework).

**AP dimension**: the **Northern Circars** (coastal Andhra) passed to the Company via the Nizam (**1766 treaty; firm grant 1823**); **Rayalaseema = the 'Ceded Districts' (1800)** — ceded by the Nizam for subsidiary-alliance costs — the very names of AP's regions are subsidiary-alliance artefacts; Company rule in Andhra ran from **Masulipatnam's factory (1611)** through Munro's ryotwari laboratory.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the conquest, dated and analysed

items: **The decisive chain:** **Plassey (1757)** — Clive's intrigue with Mir Jafar won Bengal; **Buxar (1764)** — victory over the combined Mughal-Awadh-Bengal forces gave the Company the **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar & Odisha (1765, Treaty of Allahabad)** — legal revenue power, the true foundation of empire.

**Why the British won:** superior military organisation & discipline, naval supremacy, financial strength (a subsidiary-alliance war machine funded by Indian revenue), diplomacy exploiting Indian disunity, and the fragmentation after Aurangzeb's death (1707).
**Instruments of expansion:** **Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley)** and the **Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie — Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Awadh on misgovernance)** — annexation by treaty and pretext.
**The drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji, 'Poverty and Un-British Rule'):** unrequited transfer of India's surplus to Britain — the economic-nationalist critique to cite.

**Subsidiary Alliance** — Lord Wellesley; **Doctrine of Lapse** — Lord Dalhousie.
**Drain of Wealth theory** — Dadabhai Naoroji ('Grand Old Man of India').

**Doctrine of Lapse** (Dalhousie): Satara 1848, Jaitpur/Sambalpur 1849, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854; **Awadh annexed 1856 on misgovernment**, not lapse.
Anglo-Mysore: Tipu died defending **Srirangapatnam (1799)**; Anglo-Maratha III ended 1818; **Punjab annexed 1849** after Anglo-Sikh II.
**Northern Circars** obtained from the Nizam (1766); **Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) ceded 1800** for subsidiary costs.
Company's first Andhra factory: **Masulipatnam (1611)**.
Regulating Act **1773** → Pitt's India Act **1784** → Charter Acts **1813/1833/1853** — the constitutional ladder of Company rule.

glossary.definition: The right to collect revenue and administer civil justice — granted to the Company for Bengal-Bihar-Orissa in 1765, making it sovereign in substance.
Wellesley's system binding Indian rulers to host and fund British troops, accept a Resident, and surrender foreign relations — protection at the price of sovereignty.
Dalhousie's policy of annexing states whose rulers died without a natural heir, refusing recognition to adopted successors.
The Company's (later Crown's) claimed supreme authority over Indian princely states — suzerainty above treaty text.
Rayalaseema districts ceded by the Nizam to the Company in 1800 to pay for his subsidiary force — the colonial origin of the region's name.
Naoroji's thesis that India's surplus was transferred to Britain via home charges, remittances and unrequited exports — 'the moral drain' of colonialism.

blocks.text: Land revenue was colonialism's fiscal engine (~half of Company income), and the three settlement systems were experiments in **who to make responsible for it**: the zamindar (Bengal), the individual cultivator (Madras-Bombay), or the village community (North-West). Each restructured Indian agrarian society for a century and beyond.

rows: **Cornwallis (John Shore's plan), Bengal-Bihar-Orissa** (~19% of British India)
**Thomas Munro & Alexander Read**; Madras (incl. **coastal Andhra & Rayalaseema**), Bombay (~51%)
**Holt Mackenzie (1822), R.M. Bird/James Thomason (1833)**; NW Provinces, Punjab (~30%)
**Fixed in perpetuity** (10/11 to state, 1/11 to zamindar)
Property-owning loyal gentry; predictable revenue; Whig landlordism
Utilitarian direct contact; no intermediaries; Munro's paternalism
Preserve (use) village bodies as revenue machines
**Sunset law auctions**, absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation layers, rack-rented tenants; zamindars = loyalist class
Over-assessment → debt, land alienation to moneylenders; but direct state-peasant relation (AP's agrarian DNA)
Village co-responsibility broke under over-assessment; Punjab canal-colony variant later

items: **Property revolution**: land became a **saleable, mortgageable commodity** — customary rights collapsed into contract; the moneylender entered as the new agrarian power (Deccan Riots 1875 as the symptom).

**Commercialisation**: cash revenue forced cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, groundnut in Rayalaseema) — market integration without market protection; famines intensified (1770, 1866 Orissa, 1876-78 Madras/Deccan — Rayalaseema devastated).

**Class re-formation**: Bengal — zamindar/tenant polarity (later Bengal Tenancy Acts, Permanent Settlement's slow strangulation of state finance); Madras — peasant-moneylender axis; everywhere — growth of landless labour.

**Political consequences**: agrarian grievance fed 1857 (taluqdar-sepoy Awadh nexus), peasant movements (note HCOI-038), kisan sabhas, and ultimately **zamindari abolition (Madras Estates Abolition Act 1948; the first estates taken over included Andhra zamindaris)**.

**The AP specifics**: Munro's **ryotwari was born in the Ceded Districts (Bellary-Anantapur experiments, 1800s)** before Madras-wide extension (1820); coastal Andhra had a **zamindari overlay too** (Vizianagaram, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri estates under Permanent-Settlement-type sanads, 1802-03) — so AP uniquely lived **both systems**: the delta's estate belt vs the ryotwari uplands; the **Inam lands** (tax-free grants) were a third layer, later targeted by inam abolition laws.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the three land settlements, compared

rows: Zamindar as owner; fixed revenue in perpetuity; cultivator reduced to tenant
Direct settlement with the ryot (cultivator); revenue revised periodically

items: **Common extractive logic:** high, rigid revenue demand in cash → peasant indebtedness, loss of land to moneylenders, sub-infeudation, and recurrent famines (the commercialisation of agriculture without security).

**AP link:** coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema under **Ryotwari (Munro)** — directly citable for the Andhra countryside; the deltas' later canal irrigation (Cotton's Godavari anicut) reshaped this agrarian economy.

prelimsPointers: **Permanent Settlement 1793** — Cornwallis; **Ryotwari** — Thomas Munro (Madras Presidency incl. Andhra).
**Sir Arthur Cotton** — the Godavari (Dowleswaram) anicut transformed delta agriculture.
**Permanent Settlement (1793)**: Cornwallis, Bengal; zamindar keeps **1/11th**; revenue fixed forever; 'sunset law' auctions on default.
**Ryotwari**: piloted by **Read & Munro in the Baramahal/Ceded Districts**, generalised in **Madras 1820** (Munro as Governor); direct settlement with the ryot, ~30-year revisions.
**Mahalwari**: **Holt Mackenzie's Regulation VII of 1822**, modified by **Bird/Thomason (1833)** — NW Provinces & later Punjab; village (mahal) jointly liable.
Coverage of British India: ryotwari ~**51%**, mahalwari ~30%, zamindari ~19%.
Coastal Andhra estates (Vizianagaram, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri) held **permanent sanads (1802-03)** — Madras's own Permanent-Settlement pocket.
**Madras Estates (Abolition & Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — among India's first zamindari-abolition laws, covering Andhra estates.
**Deccan Riots (1875)** against moneylenders → Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879.
mainsAngles: Compare the three land-revenue settlements on design, logic and legacy — one extractive purpose, three social engineerings.
The Permanent Settlement created property and destroyed the peasantry's customary world — discuss.
Munro's ryotwari promised the cultivator and delivered the moneylender — evaluate with the Madras/Andhra experience.
Land settlements are the deep history of Indian agrarian classes — trace the line from 1793 to zamindari abolition.
Andhra lived both zamindari and ryotwari — analyse the regional duality and its long-run consequences for AP's agrarian structure.

glossary.definition: Revenue intermediary made proprietor under the Permanent Settlement — collecting from tenants, remitting a fixed sum to the state.
The cultivating peasant — the direct settlement unit of the ryotwari system, holding a patta from the state.
A village or estate treated as one fiscal unit under mahalwari, with co-sharers jointly liable through the lambardar.
Permanent-Settlement rule auctioning zamindari estates if revenue wasn't paid by sunset of the due date — churning Bengal's landed class.
Layering of rent-collecting intermediaries between zamindar and actual tiller — Bengal counted up to a dozen tiers.
Tax-free or favourably assessed land grant (religious/service) — Madras's third tenure layer, abolished by post-independence inam legislation.

sections.heading: 1857 — causes: a century's grievances, a cartridge's spark

rows: Doctrine of Lapse (Jhansi, Nagpur, Satara); **Awadh's annexation (1856)** — the sepoys' homeland humiliated; Mughal court's planned extinction (Bahadur Shah's successors to leave the Red Fort)
Revenue over-assessment; **taluqdars of Awadh dispossessed (Summary Settlement 1856)**; deindustrialised artisans; resumption of inam/rent-free lands (Bentinck-era inquiries)
Missionary activity + reforms perceived as interference (sati abolition, widow remarriage, Religious Disabilities Act 1856 protecting converts' inheritance); racial arrogance
Sepoy pay/pension grievances; **General Service Enlistment Act 1856** (overseas service = caste loss); Indians barred above subedar; 6:1 sepoy-European ratio post-Punjab

**Greased cartridges** of the Enfield rifle (cow & pig fat) — **Mangal Pandey, Barrackpore, 29 March 1857**; Meerut sepoys court-martialled, rose **10 May 1857**, marched to Delhi, proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** emperor

blocks.text: **Spread & leaders**: Delhi (Bahadur Shah; real command **Bakht Khan**), Kanpur (**Nana Saheb**, Tantia Tope, Azimullah), Lucknow (**Begum Hazrat Mahal**), Jhansi (**Rani Lakshmibai** — died Gwalior, June 1858), Bareilly (Khan Bahadur Khan), Arrah/Bihar (**Kunwar Singh**), Faizabad (**Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah**). Recaptures: Delhi (Sept 1857, John Nicholson), Lucknow (March 1858, Campbell), Jhansi-Gwalior (Hugh Rose, June 1858); Tantia Tope's guerrilla year ended in betrayal and execution (April 1859).

sections.heading: Why it failed — and what it changed

items: **Failure causes**: no all-India spread (Punjab, Bengal, Bombay, Madras armies largely loyal — **south India, including Andhra, stayed quiet**); no unified command or plan; backward-looking symbols (restoring Mughal/Peshwa orders) vs no common positive programme; educated middle class & most princes (Scindia, Nizam — **Salar Jung kept Hyderabad loyal**) aloof; British telegraph, Crimea-freed troops, and ruthless resources.

**Nature debate (historiography)**: 'sepoy mutiny' (British official view) vs **'First War of Independence' (V.D. Savarkar, 1909)** vs 'feudal reaction' (R.C. Majumdar: 'neither first, nor national, nor war of independence') vs modern view — **a popular civil rebellion with sepoy vanguard** (S.B. Chaudhuri; Eric Stokes' peasant-armed studies): civilians outnumbered sepoys among the punished.

**Impact — the great reorganisation**: **Government of India Act 1858** — Crown rule, Secretary of State with Council, Viceroy (Canning); **Queen's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858, Allahabad)** — no annexations, religious non-interference, princes' adoption rights honoured (Lapse dead), equal-opportunity promise (honoured in breach); **Army re-engineering** — European ratio ~1:2, artillery Europeanised, 'martial races' + divide-and-rule recruitment; **princes converted to 'breakwaters in the storm'** — loyalist pillars till 1947; racial chasm deepened; conservative alliance with landlords (taluqdars restored); and the psychological legacy — 1857's memory fed later nationalism even as its methods were abandoned.

**AP note**: while the Madras Presidency stayed calm, Andhra's own anti-colonial risings ran on a different clock — the **palegar/zamindari resistances earlier (e.g., Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's Kurnool rising, 1846-47 — executed 1847)** and the tribal fituris later (Rampa 1879, Alluri 1922-24) — cite Narasimha Reddy as Rayalaseema's pre-1857 counterpart.

blocks.text: Exam tip: The examiner's favourite twist is 'why did the south stay quiet?' — answer: ryotwari's different agrarian anatomy, Madras army's composition, distance from the Gangetic grievance core — then pivot to Andhra's own separate rebellion timeline (Narasimha Reddy 1847, fituris later).

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — 1857, the interpretive debate

items: **Causes matrix:** political (Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh annexation), economic (drain, deindustrialisation, peasant/artisan distress), military (grievances, the greased **Enfield cartridge** spark), socio-religious (fear of conversion, reforms like *sati* abolition), and administrative.

**The historiographical debate:** 'a mere sepoy mutiny' (Seeley) vs 'the First War of Independence' (**V.D. Savarkar**) vs 'a feudal reaction' (R.P. Dutt) vs a restorative, backward-looking revolt lacking a unified national vision (a balanced modern view).

**Consequences:** the **Government of India Act 1858** ended Company rule → **Crown rule (Queen's Proclamation)**; end of the Mughal dynasty (Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled); reorganisation of the army; a policy of **divide and rule** and caution on social reform.
**Why it failed:** limited geographical spread, lack of unified leadership/ideology, no participation by many regions/classes, and British technological & organisational superiority.

prelimsPointers: **Government of India Act 1858** — transferred power from the Company to the Crown; first Viceroy **Lord Canning**.
**V.D. Savarkar** called 1857 'The First War of Indian Independence' (1909).
mainsAngles: 'The Revolt of 1857 was more than a sepoy mutiny but less than a national war of independence' — critically examine.

**GoI Act 1858**: Company abolished; **Secretary of State for India** with 15-member Council; Governor-General became **Viceroy (Canning first)**.
**Queen Victoria's Proclamation** read at **Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858** by Canning.

Army after 1858: European:Indian ~**1:2**, artillery exclusively European, 'martial races' recruitment.

glossary.definition: Enfield rifle cartridge rumoured coated with cow and pig fat, requiring biting — the immediate trigger of the sepoy rising.
Awadh's great landholder class, dispossessed by the 1856 Summary Settlement and restored post-1858 as loyalist allies.
The 1858 charter of Crown rule promising non-annexation, religious non-interference and equal treatment — 'the Magna Carta of Indian people' in official rhetoric.
Post-1857 recruitment doctrine favouring 'loyal' communities (Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans) while excluding the rebellion's heartland — divide-and-rule in uniform.
Tribal rising/rebellion in the Andhra agency tracts (Rampa 1879, Alluri's 1922-24) — the region's recurring form of anti-colonial revolt.
Canning's phrase for the loyal princes of 1857 — the rationale for preserving princely states as imperial pillars.
